meta.title: Physics-Informed ConvLSTM Networks for Transient Thermal Modeling of Spacecraft PCBs
meta.authorsHtml: Ismael Gallo-López<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, David González-Bárcena<sup>1</sup>, Ernesto Enfedaque-Medina<sup>1</sup>

abstract: This work integrates physical principles into neural networks for transient thermal modeling of spacecraft Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs). A Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) architecture captures spatiotemporal dynamics, with scheduled sampling to stabilise autoregressive inference over long horizons. To address the scarcity of high-fidelity thermal data in early design phases, we add a physics-informed loss term penalising violations of the nodal energy balance. Across six training-set sizes (N = 10 to N = 1000), the physics-informed variant reduces Mean Absolute Error (MAE) by 67–96% relative to an identically structured data-driven baseline, with the largest gains in the data-scarce regime (8.15 K to 0.29 K at N = 50). Worstcase errors fall below the 5 K margin typically required in spacecraft thermal analysis for N ≥200, against 12–58 K for the baseline. We additionally report a screening against three alternative architectures, a grid search over the loss weights, and a runtime comparison against the reference solver.

blocks.html: Thermal management is a fundamental challenge in spacecraft design, directly impacting the reliability and life-time of subsystems. Spaceborne components, particularly Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs), operate in extreme environments characterized by variable heat fluxes and the absence of convection [1]. Accurate transient thermal modeling is essential to ensure onboard units remain within operational limits; a maximum deviation of 5 K is a commonly adopted acceptance margin for analysis-grade thermal predictions [2].

Traditionally, thermal analysis relies on Lumped- Parameter Thermal Models (LPTM) or Finite Element Methods (FEM). While accurate, these numerical solvers are computationally expensive for large design-of-experiments or real-time onboard use [3]. Data-driven surrogate models offer a faster alternative but often struggle to generalize when training data is limited, a common scenario in space engineering [4].

This work proposes a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) approach to bridge this gap, combining a ConvL- STM architecture with a physics-informed loss and scheduled sampling. Our contributions are: (i) a ConvLSTM surrogate for transient PCB thermal fields, screened against three alternative architectures under identical data-driven training so that the contribution of the architecture is separated from that of the physics term (Section 4.1) — unlike the time-conditioned regressors dominant in the spacecraft literature, it is autoregressive and can be rolled out from an arbitrary measured state; (ii) a grid search over the loss weights replicated at six training-set sizes, quantifying how the benefit of physical regularization decays with data availability and showing that the boundary penalty is a comparably potent regularizer to the interior residual (Section 4.3); and (iii) a measured comparison of training overhead, inference time and dataset-generation cost against the reference solver (Section 4.5).

ANN surrogates for thermal problems. Neural networks have been applied to heat-transfer modelling for two decades, spanning combustion [5], solar radiation [6] and convective flow [7]; [8] surveys the field. Heng et al. [9] combined a feedforward network with the superposition principle for a parabolic solar collector, reaching a mean absolute deviation below 2 K in under a minute against three to four hours for FEM — but from 29 884 training samples. Sikka et al. [10] reached a test MSE of 2.9 × 10−3 on steady-state chip-on-spreader geometries from 3 500 samples, showing that careful feature design reduces data requirements.

Spacecraft thermal control. ANN applications in this domain date back to Martinez-Heras and Donati [11]. Reis Junior et al. [4, 12, 13] pursued real-time onboard prediction across a sequence of studies: a 7-input MLP for a CubeSat achieved sub-1 ◦C error on trained scenarios but degraded above 20 ◦C under a broader distribution; a recurrent variant on the 650 kg Amazonia-1 platform never achieved a maximum per-equipment error below 5 ◦C and was judged not operationally viable. Generalization to unseen conditions, rather than in-distribution accuracy, is the recurring failure mode.

Physics-informed and reduced-order approaches. Physics-informed machine learning [14, 15] constrains the solution to satisfy the governing equations. Tanaka and Nagai [16] introduced PINNs to spacecraft thermal analysis on a 100-node pseudo-satellite with a three-term loss (data, steady-state heat balance, boundary conditions), reporting 3.7–5.5 K average error with maxima above 8.0 K; trainingset size was not quantified. The same group combined this loss with Proper Orthogonal Decomposition [17] for data reduction [18], reaching 0.6–2.0 K average nodal deviation with inference in 0.13–0.17 s against 5 756–7 562 s for the full solver over 500 cases. Yamashita et al. [19] extended POD reduction with RNN and LSTM heads (1.16 K mean, 10.7 K maximum for the LSTM over a full orbit).

Positioning. Three gaps motivate this work. First, the field is dominated by MLP and POD-projected architectures that discard the spatial topology of the temperature field; ConvLSTM [20] preserves it natively, which matters where errors concentrate at heaters and interfaces. Second, existing PINN work here [16, 18] enforces a steady-state balance, whereas our transient residual constrains the trajectory at every rollout step. Third, none of the cited studies systematically varies the training-set size, so the central claim of physics-informed methods — data efficiency — remains largely unquantified in this application, which we address with a grid search across six values of N.

The case study is a simplified PCB represented as a homogeneous square plate discretized into a 13 × 13 Cartesian grid. Each node represents a thermal mass with localized heater inputs and radiative exchange with the environment. The governing transient heat balance at node i is described by Equation (1):

blocks.html: where ρ, c, Vi are density, specific heat, and volume; Kij and Eij are conductive and radiative couplings; and Qi is the heater power.

The dataset was generated with a numerical solver of Equation (1) at ∆t = 1 s over a 650 s horizon, then downsampled to ∆t = 10 s, a resolution selected by a prior sweep over ∆t ∈{1, . . . , 100} s as the best compromise between rollout length and error accumulation. Each of the 3 050 sequences samples a distinct scenario: four heater powers from U(0.5, 1.5) W, four interface temperatures and one environment temperature from U(270, 320) K, with uniform Tinit = 298 K. The pool splits into 2 500 training, 500 validation and 50 test sequences; the subsets studied below (N = 10 to 1000) are nested draws from the training partition, with Nval = N/5, and all variants share the same test set, normalization statistics and random seeds.

We employ a ConvLSTM architecture [20] to capture both spatial correlations (via convolutions) and temporal evolution (via LSTM gates), preserving the spatial topology that standard MLPs discard when flattening the grid [21]. To enforce physical consistency, the network is trained with a composite loss:

where LMSE is the data-fitting error, Lphysics is the mean squared residual of Equation (1) evaluated by finite differences on the predicted outputs, penalising non-physical energy generation or loss, and Lbnd enforces boundary conditions at interface and radiative edge nodes.

Figure 1 summarises the resulting pipeline, including the scheduled-sampling feedback described next. The network uses two ConvLSTM layers with 64 hidden channels each, a 3×3 ReLU kernel, six input channels, and is trained with Adam (batch 64, initial LR 0.01, paired with decay: factor 0.1 at 10 epochs’ patience, early stopping at 100).

All scalar channels are standardized to zero mean and unit variance. Crucially, we augment the input with binary masks marking heater and interface locations (Figure 1): without them the ConvLSTM cannot distinguish “zero power” (active heater, off) from “no information” (empty space), leading to gradient instability.

The model is trained autoregressively. To mitigate exposure bias—where the model relies too heavily on groundtruth history during training but fails when feeding back its own predictions at inference—we employ Scheduled Sampling [22], with the probability of feeding ground truth at epoch i decaying linearly as ϵi = max(0, 1 −i/K), K = 200. This forces the model to learn to correct its own accumulated errors, substantially improving stability over the 650 s window.

Models are evaluated autoregressively over the full horizon on the held-out test set. We report MAE averaged over all nodes, timesteps and cases, and the maximum pointwise error over the same population. Improvement is (MAEbase −MAE)/MAEbase. The baseline is the identical ConvLSTM trained with λphy = λbnd = 0, so architecture, capacity, optimizer and schedule are held fixed. Loss weights were selected by grid search with λMSE = 1 and λphy, λbnd ∈{0, 10−7, . . . , 1, 102, 103}, repeated independently for each N; only relative magnitudes matter, since with all weights at 1 the boundary term saturates the optimizer.

Before introducing the physics term, four architectures were compared under identical MSE-only training on a shorter 50 s rollout at ∆t = 1 s over 1 000 test cases (not numerically comparable to the main results, but sufficient to establish that architecture choice, not only the loss, drives performance): a feedforward MLP with explicit physical inputs (MAE 2.977 K, max 24.74 K), a spatio-temporal regressor with explicit time conditioning (4.869 K, 68.62 K), a CNN encoder with conditional spatio-temporal decoder (3.977 K, 50.83 K), and the ConvLSTM (0.114 K, 11.09 K).

The ConvLSTM outperforms the alternatives by more than an order of magnitude in MAE. Beyond accuracy, it was the only candidate that could be driven autoregressively from its own outputs: the other three require a uniform initial condition and an explicit time coordinate, which precludes rollout from an arbitrary measured state and hence any onboard estimation use. Its maximum error of 11.09 K nevertheless exceeded the 5 K margin, motivating the physical constraints below.

Table 1 reports the best physics-informed configuration against the baseline at each training-set size. The physics-informed model dominates at every N, but the margin varies sharply. In the ultra-low data regime the baseline fails outright: at N = 50 it reaches 8.15 K MAE with a maximum error of 53.90 K, against 0.29 K and 8.28 K for the physics-informed model. The improvement decays as data becomes plentiful, to 67.1% at N = 1000; across the six sizes the Pearson correlation between N and improvement is −0.849, evidencing diminishing returns rather than a uniform benefit.

blocks.html: The maximum-error column is arguably more relevant than the mean. The baseline never satisfies the 5 K margin at any training-set size tested, peaking at 57.7 K; the physics-informed model satisfies it for N ≥200. This mirrors the failure mode reported for spacecraft ANN surrogates in Section 2, where mean accuracy was acceptable but worst-case deviations disqualified the model operationally. Temporally, the baseline error grows within the first 100 s of rollout and then oscillates without recovering, the signature of compounding autoregressive error, while every physics-informed configuration in the grid search stays flat across the full 650 s horizon.

The grid search permits a direct ablation, since λphy = 0 and λbnd = 0 are both included in the sweep. At N = 400, the interior residual alone (λphy = 1, λbnd = 0) yields 0.122 K (+91.0%) and the boundary term alone (λphy = 0, λbnd = 10−3) yields 0.128 K (+90.5%), against 0.126 K (+90.7%) for the best combined configuration and 1.353 K for the baseline with both terms removed. The same pattern holds at N = 50 (+93.0% and +90.9% individually, +96.4% combined) and at N = 1000 (+49.2% and +58.2%, +67.1% combined). The boundary penalty is therefore not a secondary refinement, as we had assumed: constraining the edge nodes, where the steepest gradients and largest errors occur, is nearly as effective as constraining the interior. Their combination is consistently best, but the marginal contribution of the second term is small.

blocks.html: The optimal weights are regime-dependent rather than universal: λphy = 10−2 at N = 50, 1 at N = 400, 10−5 at N = 1000. What generalises is the failure mode, not the optimum. Values of λbnd ≥1 degrade performance below the baseline at every N, and at λbnd ≥102 the MAE exceeds 11 K as the boundary term saturates the optimizer. The weights should be treated as tuned hyperparameters, with the caveat that over-weighting the physical terms is more damaging than under-weighting them.

Beyond global metrics, it is critical for spacecraft operations to quantify uncertainty at specific components. Figure 2 shows the predicted temperature at a central node (x = 6, y = 6) for a test case in the N = 400 regime, with 95% confidence bands computed over 100 independent test cases. The physics-informed model tracks the ground truth closely with narrow bands, whereas the purely data-driven baseline exhibits wide oscillating intervals: at a heater node in the N = 10 regime the mean confidence span contracts from 83.6 K to 20.9 K under physical regularization, a 75% reduction. This suggests the approach is suitable for operational limit checking (e.g. triggering safe mode if T > Tmax), the bounds providing a usable safety margin rather than an uninformative one.
Figure 3 shows the spatial distribution of errors at N =

400. Errors concentrate near heaters and boundaries where gradients are steepest, with the worst-case node at the (0,0) corner interface, but physics-informed training keeps these maxima bounded at 4.29 K, ensuring no “hot spots” are artificially created or ignored. The corresponding corner maximum at N = 50 is 8.28 K, so the spatial concentration of error is a structural feature the physics term bounds but does not eliminate.

The physics terms are not free: at N = 50 training grows from 0.52 to 6.67 minutes, a 13× overhead. Inference cost is unchanged, since both variants share the same parameter count and graph, and dataset generation costs 0.222 s per case.

We report the solver comparison without inflation: the surrogate is not faster, at 0.045–0.056 s per case against 0.044 s for the solver, a speedup of 0.8–1.0×. The reference solver avoids computing view factors, normally the dominant cost in spacecraft thermal analysis [3], so a simplified 169-node plate is close to the worst case for a surrogate; the order-of-magnitude speedups reported for larger models [18, 19] scale with the cost of the solver being replaced.

In purely data-driven deep learning, the model approximates the manifold of valid thermal states solely from training points; when data is sparse it overfits the few observed trajectories and fails on unseen boundary conditions, which is exactly the baseline behaviour at N ≤50. The residual terms constrain the search space to solutions satisfying Equation (1), acting as an unlimited source of unlabelled supervision: even for a heater configuration never seen, the loss penalises predictions that create or destroy energy. Hence the 96.4% reduction at N = 50, and its decay to 67.1% at N = 1000, where the dataset alone already covers the relevant manifold.

Safety and Reliability: In spacecraft thermal control, average accuracy matters less than ensuring no component exceeds its qualification limits. The physics-informed model clamps predictions to physically plausible values, suppressing the large localised excursions that disqualified earlier ANN surrogates [4]: its maximum error falls below the 5 K margin for N ≥200 while the baseline never does.

Operational Feasibility: Two applications follow from constant-time, differentiable evaluation rather than raw speed. Rapid design trades benefit from GPU-batched evaluation of thousands of heater configurations, amortising per-case cost across the batch. Onboard virtual sensors exploit the autoregressive formulation: unlike the timeconditioned regressors of Section 4.1, the ConvLSTM can be initialised from an arbitrary measured field and rolled forward to estimate temperatures at unmeasured locations.

The residual in Lphysics is evaluated with the same discrete energy balance, and the same coupling coefficients Kij and Eij, that the reference solver uses to generate the training data. The physical term therefore encodes exact knowledge of the data-generating process rather than an approximate prior, and part of the observed gain follows from that consistency: the network is, in effect, being told the solver it is learning to imitate. The reported improvements are thus best read as an upper bound obtained under perfectly specified physics; how the method degrades when Kij and Eij are uncertain, as they invariably are before thermal balance testing, is not answered here. We nonetheless consider the term to retain value, since it is the only mechanism that constrains predictions at operating points the dataset does not cover, and the N ≤200 results show it doing so where the data demonstrably cannot. Quantifying robustness to perturbed couplings and out-of-distribution configurations is the first priority for follow-up work.

Three further limitations bound the scope. The geometry is a fixed homogeneous plate with static heater placement, so a different board requires retraining. Initial conditions are uniform, though a separate baseline study with Tinit sampled per node found comparable accuracy. Finally, ∆t is fixed at training time; treating it as an input feature, or moving to continuous-time formulations such as neural ODEs [23], Fourier Neural Operators [24] or DeepONet [25], would lift that constraint. Training on thermographic measurements would relax the dependence on synthetic data, and Graph Neural Networks offer a more natural representation of irregular geometries for system-level modelling, currently under investigation in parallel work [26].

A transient energy-balance residual in the loss of a ConvLSTM surrogate reduces MAE by 67–96% relative to an identically structured data-driven baseline, with worst-case errors below the 5 K acceptance margin for N ≥200 where the baseline never is. The benefit decays with data availability (r = −0.849), and the boundary penalty proves nearly as effective as the interior residual. The cost falls entirely on training. The principal open question is robustness to misspecified couplings, which experiments sharing physics between the loss and the data generator cannot address.
